I am a physicist working on the experimental study of transition-metal oxides,
currently based in the [Oxide Nanophysics group](https://icn2.cat/en/oxide-nanophysics-group)
at the Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology (ICN2) in Barcelona.
My work sits at the interface between materials growth, low-temperature electrical
transport, and the instrumentation that makes those measurements possible.

## What I work on

Much of my day-to-day revolves around **cryogenic transport measurements** of
oxide thin films and heterostructures — resistance-versus-temperature curves,
Hall effect, and field-dependent transport down to low temperatures and under
applied magnetic field. I am particularly interested in **metal–insulator
transitions** and how they are shaped by strain, dimensionality, and interface
effects in systems such as nickelates and doped titanates.

Alongside the physics, I build a good deal of the **measurement infrastructure**
I rely on: instrument drivers for lock-in amplifiers, temperature controllers
and magnet power supplies, a multi-threaded control application for coordinating
an experiment end to end, and Python tooling for extracting physical quantities
from the raw data. I find that caring about the measurement chain — not just the
final plot — tends to pay off in the quality of the science.

## Background

I completed my undergraduate and master's studies in physics at the Universidad
Nacional Mayor de San Marcos in Lima, with a focus on condensed matter and
materials science, working on thin-film growth by sputtering and pulsed laser
deposition. That experimental grounding — sample preparation, X-ray diffraction,
magnetometry — is what I now bring to the study of oxide nanostructures.

I am always glad to talk with people working on oxide electronics, metal–insulator
